Rare earth elements are actually not that rare, they are usually not valuable enough to bother to dig up. Many of them are obtained as a byproduct of producing more common elements, such as in iron or nickel mining, for example. Rare elements are often found in combination with other rare minerals in the same deposit. For example, in the Sudbury nickel mines, the main product is nickel, but those mines also produce gold, silver, etc, in smaller quantities. The same is true for most mines.

That said, the rare metals, including the better known ones such a gold, silver, etc, are most often byproducts of the earths core, and as such are frequently found in mountainous terrain, especially near volcanic activity. Plate tectonics also plays a roll in bringing to the surface earth which was previously located much deeper underground. This is one of the reasons that you will often find mining activities clustered around fault lines. Japan, as a volcanic island chain, is probably teaming with rare earth elements.
